cards.title: A family tree of software job titles

depth.text: someone mapped how **software job titles** branch, vanish, and return, from early computing to AI

The **104-title tree** runs from “Computer” (a person, not a machine) to “AI Agent / Context Engineer,” with solid arrows for titles growing from parents and dashed arrows for influence or common career moves. It shows titles **splitting and rejoining**: the web developer split into front-end and back-end, then the two joined back up as “full-stack.”

cards.camps: Some commenters say job titles are mostly meaningless or not worth fussing over; others argue titles need careful mapping because the same title can mean different work across companies and over time.

cards.title: Project Zero will disclose vulnerabilities 90 days after reporting

depth.text: **Project Zero** will give vendors less time to fix bugs before **publishing them**
The new **Full 90** policy discloses vulnerabilities 90 days after they’re reported to the vendor; it moves to **60 days** on February 2, 2027, and **30 days** on January 3, 2028.

cards.camps: Some say vendors like Ubuntu need more time; others want disclosure to happen right away to pressure companies into fixing bugs.

cards.title: Advancing science and engineering with Antigravity's /teamwork

depth.text: Google says its **multi-agent tools** have tackled **open research problems** and are now available to developers

It pairs parallel exploration with **checks** that test whether candidate solutions work. Examples include a proof of the **Courtade–Kumar conjecture** and a machine-checked formalization of the Weil conjectures spanning about **1.8 million lines of Lean**.

cards.title: We're Asking an Appeals Court to Require a Warrant for ALPR Searches

depth.text: EFF is asking an appeals court to require **warrants** for police **license-plate searches**

In United States v. Sturdivant, officers searched **Flock and ELSAG databases** and found the defendant’s car had been tracked near robbery sites. EFF and the ACLU argue that the network can reveal drivers’ **past movements**, making that tracking a **Fourth Amendment search**.

cards.camps: Two camps: some commenters want ALPR data collection sharply limited or stopped; others see value in using it to investigate crimes, but want access tightly controlled.

cards.title: How did Woz write the Apple 1 BASIC before building the computer?

depth.text: Woz wrote Apple 1 **BASIC by hand**, but commenters still wonder how it got into **ROM**

A commenter says Woz's **handwritten interpreter** is familiar, but asks how it got from paper into **ROM**. Another sketches a possible path using a 6502 cross-assembler and monitor program, then says they have no idea if that's what Woz did.

comments.text: What Woz did was the default way of writing assembly language programs for owners of 8-bit computers (mostly hobbyists). You didn't have money for a second machine, so you wrote your program on paper, you entered it then tested it in situ. Mostly you got it right, as doing it on paper was slow and meant you had the opportunity to put lots of thought into it. 8-bit instruction sets were simple…

I don’t know about other people, but back in the early 80s, I spent a lot of time writing code (mostly assembler, some BASIC and other dead languages) with pencil on paper for various reasons: sometimes I preferred it, sometimes I was writing code for computers I only had access to in labs or at school. There were even pre-made paper forms for writing code, like the IBM COBOL program sheets and…

Back in the 80s I wrote an assembler and a simulator for a custom DSP before the board was manufactured (it was the 80s so several chips were required), and our team wrote and tested code for it before the board was ready. When the board was ready, we wound up having to modify the assembler and simulator because some control signals were wired backwards and it was easier to just change the…

I've never "assembled by hand" but I can believe it and imagine it. As a kid I did write basic code by hand and would type it into my Timex Sinclair with no ability to save it because we could not get the tape cassette to work to save it. So for the first few weeks it would all disappear when you turned the computer off. What a blessing it was to get that cassette to work and be able to save and…

Follow-up question: how did Woz get BASIC into ROM? The handwritten interpreter is fairly common knowledge since Woz has told that story many times, but I don't recall any accounts of how he bridged the gap from paper to silicon. All of the discussion about the machine language monitor doesn't really address the question. At best, it moves the question from programming a ROM for BASIC to…

glossary.GPU: Graphics Processing Unit: the chip part that draws images and video.
glossary.circular financing: A setup where money supplied by one business loops back to it through another business's purchases.
glossary.wafer: A thin round slice of material that computer chips are made from.
glossary.backstop: A promise to provide money if a deal cannot get enough funding elsewhere.
glossary.MSRP: Manufacturer's Suggested Retail Price: the price a maker recommends shops charge for a product.
glossary.SRE: Site Reliability Engineering: work focused on keeping online services running and fixing them when they break.
glossary.DevOps: The work of getting software released and keeping it running.
glossary.platform engineering: Work on shared tools and systems that help other developers build and run software.
glossary.full-stack: Building both the parts of an app people use and the behind-the-scenes parts that make it work.
glossary.prompt engineer: A person who writes instructions for AI models to get useful results.
glossary.FDE: Forward Deployed Engineer: a software engineer who works with a customer to get software working for that customer's needs.
glossary.MLM: Multi-level marketing: A business where members recruit others and may earn money from what those recruits do.
glossary.commission: Money someone earns when a booking or sale brings in money.
glossary.ghost jobs: Job ads for roles that aren't actually available or may not exist.
glossary.LLM: Large Language Model: an AI trained on lots of writing so it can take written questions and produce written answers.
glossary.patch gap: The time between a security fix being released and a user installing the update.
glossary.soak time: Extra time after a fix is made for it to roll out to users.
glossary.JAX: A software tool for writing calculations that can run on different kinds of computers.
glossary.MLA: Multi-head Latent Attention: a way for a language model to keep a smaller memory of earlier words while it writes.
glossary.mixture-of-experts: A model split into specialist parts, with only some parts used for each piece of text it produces.
glossary.auxiliary loss: An extra training penalty that encourages the model to spread work across its experts.
glossary.MTP: Multi-token prediction: training a model to guess more than one piece of text ahead at a time.
glossary.multi-agent system: A setup where several AI helpers each work on part of a task.
glossary.falsifier: A check designed to show that a proposed answer does not work.
glossary.formalization: Writing mathematics in a precise form that a computer can check.
glossary.Lean 4: A programming language and tool for checking that mathematical reasoning follows rules.
glossary.ALPR: Automatic license plate recognition: technology that reads vehicle license plates from camera images.
glossary.amicus brief: A written argument from an outside group giving a court its view on a case.
glossary.Fourth Amendment: The part of the US Constitution that protects people from unreasonable searches and seizures.
glossary.warrant: A judge's written permission for a search or seizure.
glossary.ROM: Read-Only Memory: information a computer can read but is not normally meant to change.
glossary.6502 cross-assembler: A tool for turning a program into the numeric instructions a 6502 can run.
glossary.monitor program: A small program for looking at and changing memory, then running code stored there.
glossary.machine code: The low-level instructions a computer's processor can run directly.
glossary.API: Application Programming Interface: a way for one program to ask another for information or actions.
glossary.Fact Graph: A structure that keeps related facts together and can handle a return with some answers still missing.
glossary.XML: Extensible Markup Language: a way to label pieces of information so computers can store and exchange them.
glossary.JVM: Java Virtual Machine: software that runs programs built for Java's runtime.
glossary.transpiled: Rewritten from one kind of code into another before the program runs.
glossary.PII: Personally Identifiable Information: details that could identify someone, such as an email or phone number.
glossary.terminal-native: Made to run inside a terminal, the text window people use to type commands.
glossary.idle game: A game where progress or rewards can build up while you wait or do little.
glossary.Rust: A programming language; commenters say 37signals used it for the Hey backend.
glossary.ratatui: A Rust tool for building text-based screens inside a terminal.
glossary.RP: Research points: points the game says are needed to unlock things.
glossary.Claude Code hooks: A way for Claude Code to send an agent's replies into the game as messages.
glossary.slopware: A dismissive word for software someone thinks is low-quality or carelessly made.
glossary.application switcher: Software that lets you move between running apps without closing each one.
glossary.heap zone: A separate section of computer memory set aside for one app.
glossary.low memory: A reserved part of the Mac's memory where the system kept information apps needed.
